title: Father, forgive them (Luke 23:32–43)
hook: he forgives his executioners and promises paradise to a dying thief
carry: they know not what they do

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daughters of Jerusalem, and Jesus turning to comfort them. Your line was weep not for me. Who did you turn toward, even in a hard week? Day five hundred eighty-six.

A Persian king's garden. High walls around it, and inside, water running in channels, fruit trees, shade, quiet. The old Persian word for an enclosure like that passed into Greek, and in the Greek translation of Genesis it was used for the garden God planted in Eden. Hold that picture of a walled garden. Now put it next to the ugliest place in the story: a hill outside the city that Luke calls the place of the skull. Three crosses. Jesus in the middle, a criminal on each side. Today's word comes from the garden, and it is spoken on that hill.

Luke gives us two sayings from the cross that no other Gospel has. The first comes as the soldiers are nailing him there, in the King James words: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." Then they divide his clothes by casting lots. He's praying for the people doing it, while they're doing it. A careful note: this prayer is missing from some of the oldest manuscripts of Luke and present in many others. Christians have treasured it for many centuries either way. The second comes later. The crowd stares. The leaders sneer. The soldiers mock. One of the criminals hanging beside him joins in: aren't you the Christ? Save yourself and us. But the other one tells him to stop. We deserve this, he says. This man has done nothing wrong. And then he turns his head toward Jesus: "Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom." Not save me. Just remember me. And Jesus answers: "Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." Paradise: the walled garden, Eden restored, life with God. Promised to a man with no time left to do a single good deed. Christians read the word in more than one way. Many hear it as the soul's rest with God right after death, before the final resurrection. Some groups place the comma after today, I tell you today, and read the promise as future. Ancient Greek manuscripts had little punctuation, so the comma is a translator's choice. All of them hear the same heart in it: the last person Jesus speaks to on the cross, apart from his Father, is a criminal, and he says yes.
screen: then, large: `TO DAY SHALT THOU BE WITH ME IN PARADISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive someone who doesn't know better. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who hurt you without really understanding what they were doing. A parent doing their best with what they had. A kid who said something cruel. A stranger who cut you off. Hold them in your mind. Notice that they didn't see the whole picture. If you pray, you can say Jesus's words for them: Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do. If you don't, simply try loosening your grip on it, even a little. The bell holds the time.
Paradise. From an old Persian word for a walled garden, used in Greek for Eden; the place Jesus promises the dying thief, today.
Your line: they know not what they do. Today, when someone hurts you without seeing it, try saying this line in your head before you answer. Day five hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: On Good Friday many churches hold services on the seven last words of Christ from the cross; the first two are Father, forgive them, and the promise of paradise to the penitent thief.

original.note: Greek, borrowed from Old Persian: an enclosed park or garden. used in the Greek translation of Genesis for Eden.

trapdoor: what you thought: paradise means heaven, a perfect beach.
what it means: the walled garden of life with God, promised to a dying man who only asked to be remembered.
what a scholar hears: paradeisos comes from Old Persian for an enclosure; the comma in 23:43 is a translator's choice; and 23:34a is missing from some early manuscripts.

notes: Paradise from Old Persian (Avestan pairi-daēza), 'enclosure', via Greek paradeisos; used in the Septuagint for the garden of Eden (Genesis 2:8). Confirm.
Luke 23:34a is absent from some early manuscripts (e.g. P75, Vaticanus) and present in many others. Confirm the phrasing.
Comma placement in 23:43: some groups (e.g. Jehovah's Witnesses, many Seventh-day Adventists) read 'I tell you today'. The script says 'some groups' without naming them. Confirm fairness.
Luke calls the place 'Calvary' in the KJV (Greek Kranion, skull). The hook says 'the place of the skull'. Confirm.
'The last person Jesus speaks to on the cross, apart from his Father' holds for Luke's account (23:46 is addressed to the Father). Confirm.
